html:
The Papal States were the lands in central Italy ruled directly by the pope as a king, from 756 to 1870. At their largest they ran across the peninsula from Rome and Lazio through Umbria and the Marche to Bologna and the Romagna. On the map they appear from 800 to 1815.

They began when the Frankish king Pepin the Short beat the Lombards and handed their conquests around Rome and Ravenna to the pope, the Donation of Pepin. In return the popes backed the Frankish kings, and in 800 Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor.

For most of the Middle Ages papal rule was weak. Roman nobles and local lords held the towns, and from 1309 to 1377 the popes lived in Avignon, in the Avignon Papacy. Renaissance popes took real control. Julius II led his own armies in the field and also paid for the Sistine Chapel ceiling. Ferrara was added in 1598.

The end came in stages:

  • Napoleon annexed the lands to France and held the pope prisoner.
  • The Congress of Vienna restored them in 1815.
  • In 1860 most of them joined the new kingdom of Italy, led by Piedmont-Sardinia.
  • In 1870 Italian troops took Rome itself.

The popes refused to accept the loss until the Lateran Treaty of 1929 created the tiny Vatican City.
